Seminar Title:

Numerical investigation of charged micro- and nano-plastic depositions in human respiratory airways

Seminar Type:

Department:

Kishore Singh Patel

Abstract:

Deposition of nano- and micro-sized plastics (NMPs) in the human lung poses severe health implications, and their long-term effects are yet to be understood. Long-term accumulation and deposition dynamics of these NMPs are not fully understood. The present study investigates the effects of particle size, shape, and electrostatic charge on particle transport and deposition in human respiratory airways using computational fluid dynamics (CFD) coupled with the discrete phase model (DPM). An Eulerian&ndashLagrangian framework is employed to simulate airflow and individual particle trajectories, accounting for aerodynamic drag, gravity, and electrostatic image forces. Two three-dimensional (3D) airway geometries are developed: an idealized Weibel model extending from generation G0 to G14 and a realistic computed tomography (CT)-scan-based model extending up to G7. Spherical, cylindrical, and tetrahedral particles are considered using appropriate drag formulations and shape factors. An unstructured tetrahedral mesh with near-wall inflation layers is generated, followed by a grid-independence assessment. At peak inspiration, the airflow field exhibits a maximum velocity of 1.71 m/s, with local acceleration near airway bifurcations and a general reduction in velocity towards distal generations as airflow divides among successive branches. Further, the pressure field reaches a maximum of 1.5 Pa in the proximal airways, then progressively decreases toward distal generations due to viscous friction and resistance within the branching passages. An electrostatic force user-defined function (UDF) is developed in ANSYS Fluent 2023 R1 to incorporate particle&ndashwall electrostatic interactions. The formulation is evaluated using a 3D cylindrical duct and compared with published numerical and analytical results. Particle diameters of 1&ndash10 &microm are investigated under different charge conditions. The approach is subsequently applied to the idealized Weibel model. A realistic 3D airway geometry and its 3D-printed counterpart are also developed to support further computational and experimental investigations. Future work will examine particle deposition, retention, and accumulation and incorporate physics-informed neural networks (PINNs).
